name: Basilar artery
summary: Formed by the union of the vertebral arteries at the lower border of the pons, the basilar artery runs in the midline groove of the pons to its upper border, where it divides into the two posterior cerebral arteries. Along the way it gives the anterior inferior cerebellar, labyrinthine, pontine and superior cerebellar arteries. Because it feeds the whole pons and the midbrain, occlusion is one of the most devastating strokes, ranging from crossed brainstem syndromes to the locked-in state or coma.

anatomy.location: Lies in the prepontine cistern on the anterior surface of the pons, in the basilar sulcus, between the two abducens nerves at its origin and the two oculomotor nerves at its termination in the interpeduncular cistern.

subdivisions.name: Paramedian branches
subdivisions.note: medial pons: corticospinal fibers, pontine nuclei, medial lemniscus, abducens and facial nuclei

subdivisions.name: Basilar tip
subdivisions.note: P1 segments, thalamoperforators, superior cerebellar arteries

relations.lateral: abducens nerves inferiorly and oculomotor nerves superiorly

function: Supplies the entire pons, the superior cerebellum, the inner ear (via the labyrinthine artery), and through its terminal branches the midbrain, thalamus and occipital lobes.

bestView.label: basilar trunk on the clivus in front of the pons
midline flow void in the prepontine cistern
basilar tip in the interpeduncular cistern

imaging.normalAppearance: A single midline flow void in front of the pons on every axial T2 slice through the pons and a smooth tube on sagittal T1. On non-contrast CT the artery lies on the clivus; a dense basilar suggests acute thrombus. CTA shows the whole vessel from the vertebral confluence to the tip.

pathology.finding: Absent contrast in a segment of the basilar with bilateral pontine, cerebellar, thalamic and occipital infarcts on DWI depending on the level; the hyperdense basilar sign on plain CT is an early clue.
pathology.timing: Hyperdense basilar visible at once; DWI lesions evolve over hours; recanalisation therapy is time-critical

pathology.finding: A wedge of restricted diffusion in one paramedian half of the pons reaching the ventral surface, from branch atheromatous disease of a paramedian perforator.
Saccular aneurysm at the bifurcation projecting upward into the interpeduncular cistern; may compress the oculomotor nerves or the midbrain.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: CTA immediately when a brainstem stroke is suspected; DWI for extent; DSA for treatment planning

lesionEffects.deficit: Quadriparesis with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements (locked-in)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Bilateral ventral pontine infarction sparing the tegmentum and midbrain

lesionEffects.deficit: Crossed syndromes: ipsilateral cranial nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis
lesionEffects.mechanism: Unilateral paramedian pontine infarct catching the abducens or facial nucleus/fascicle and the corticospinal tract
Pontine tegmentum and reticular activating system

lesionEffects.deficit: Top-of-the-basilar syndrome: somnolence, vertical gaze palsy, hallucinations, hemianopia
lesionEffects.mechanism: Embolus at the bifurcation involving thalamus, midbrain and occipital lobes

examination: Assess consciousness, pupils, corneal reflexes and eye movements in every stuporous patient
Ask about preceding vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria and drop attacks (basilar TIAs)
pearls: Bilateral or crossed signs with altered consciousness mean the basilar artery until proven otherwise; call for CTA
Locked-in patients are awake: examine vertical eye movements and blinking before assuming coma

pitfalls: Basilar occlusion may present with fluctuating symptoms or apparent psychiatric change over hours before collapse
A dolichoectatic basilar can compress cranial nerves or cause perforator strokes without occlusion
